title: Interview Transcription and Speaker Separation
answer: Interview transcription and speaker separation covers the conversion of recorded interviews into written text and the labelling of who spoke when. It sits inside qualitative analysis and mixed methods, where transcripts become the raw material for coding, thematic analysis, conversation analysis and case comparison. The work includes verbatim transcription, time alignment, speaker diarization, handling overlapping speech, accents, dialects and background noise. The site's library holds 135 research papers, and this topic draws on methods from linguistics, speech processing and social research.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on audio capture, storage and compute. A typical setup uses recorders or conferencing tools, local or cloud storage, and software that can run automatic speech recognition and diarization models. Graphics processors speed up large models, while smaller interviews can be processed on a laptop. Sensitive interviews often stay on encrypted local machines or private servers with access controls, because audio and transcripts can identify people.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The workflow starts with recording and ingesting audio, then preprocessing for noise, channel separation and format conversion. Automatic speech recognition produces a draft transcript, and diarization assigns speaker turns, which are then aligned and labelled. A researcher checks the draft against the audio, corrects names, technical terms and overlaps, and marks non-speech sounds. The corrected transcript is imported into qualitative data analysis software for coding, memoing and mixed methods linkage. Quality checks may include a second pass, timestamp verification and documented decisions about verbatim versus edited transcription.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk centre on consent, confidentiality and provenance. Participants should understand how recordings and transcripts will be stored, shared and quoted, and ethics review often governs this. Risks include misidentification of speakers, re-identification from voice or content, and unequal error rates for accents, dialects and noisy settings. Provenance requires keeping the original audio, versioning transcripts, and recording which model, settings and edits produced each version. This site links to original papers rather than secondary summaries, which supports that provenance chain.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward better handling of overlapping speech, code-switching, low-resource languages and long recordings. On-device and privacy-preserving transcription are growing, which matters for sensitive interviews. Diarization is improving with end-to-end models, and transcripts are increasingly linked to video, survey and sensor data in mixed methods designs. Automated coding suggestions may speed up early analysis, but interpretation and reflexivity remain human tasks. Standards for reporting model settings, error rates and speaker labels are likely to become more common.
